name: Peter
bio:
Simon, called Peter, was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee when Jesus called him and his brother Andrew to follow him and become "fishers of men"; they immediately left their nets to do so (Matthew 4:18-20). John's Gospel records that Andrew, newly a disciple of Jesus, first brought his brother Simon to him; Jesus, on seeing him, renamed him Cephas, meaning "a stone" (John 1:40-42). His prominent, often impulsive role among the disciples is told in detail in the chapters ahead. Luke's account adds that this call came after Jesus taught from Peter's boat and then told him, despite a fruitless night of fishing, to let down his nets again; the catch was so great it nearly sank both boats, and Peter, astonished, fell at Jesus's knees crying, "Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord," before Jesus reassured him and he left everything to follow (Luke 5:1-11). When Jesus entered Peter's house, he healed Peter's mother-in-law of a fever with a touch (Matthew 8:14-15). When Jesus walked on the water during a storm, Peter asked to join him and briefly walked on the water himself, but began to sink when fear overtook his faith; Jesus caught him and gently rebuked his doubt (Matthew 14:28-31). When the disciples asked for clarification on Jesus's teaching that defilement comes from the heart rather than food, Peter was the one who asked him to explain the saying (Matthew 15:15-20).

 At Caesarea Philippi, when Jesus asked who the disciples believed he was, Peter declared him "the Christ, the Son of the living God"; Jesus blessed him for this Father-given revelation, declared he would build his church on this foundation, and gave him the keys of the kingdom of heaven. When Jesus then predicted his own coming death in Jerusalem, Peter rebuked him for it, and Jesus sharply called him "Satan" for thinking only in human terms (Matthew 16:13-23).

 Peter witnessed Jesus's transfiguration with Moses and Elijah, offering to build shelters for them before a voice from heaven interrupted. Later, when Capernaum's tax collectors questioned him about the temple tax, Jesus had him catch a fish with a coin in its mouth to pay it for them both (Matthew 17:1-27). Peter asked Jesus how many times he should forgive a repeatedly sinning brother, suggesting seven; Jesus answered "seventy times seven," teaching boundless forgiveness (Matthew 18:21-22). Peter asked Jesus what reward the disciples would receive for having given up everything to follow him; Jesus promised them thrones in the age to come, and that the last would be first (Matthew 19:27-30).

 Jesus sent Peter and John specifically to prepare the Passover meal for the Last Supper (Luke 22:8), and at the table warned him that Satan desired to sift him like wheat, but that he had prayed for his faith to endure, so that once restored he could strengthen the other disciples (Luke 22:31-32). At the Last Supper, Peter confidently insisted he would never desert Jesus even if everyone else did, but Jesus predicted he would deny him three times before dawn. At Gethsemane, Peter was among the three disciples Jesus took deeper into the garden, though he fell asleep each time Jesus checked on them. After Jesus's arrest, Peter followed at a distance into the high priest's courtyard, but when questioned three times about his association with Jesus, he denied knowing him each time, growing more emphatic with each denial; when the rooster crowed as predicted, Peter remembered Jesus's words and wept bitterly (Matthew 26:33-75). When Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James reported that Jesus's tomb was empty, Peter ran to see for himself, and found only the linen cloths left behind. Later that day, the risen Jesus appeared to Peter personally, as two disciples returning from Emmaus learned when they found the eleven already saying the Lord had appeared to Simon (Luke 24:1-12, 34). When Jesus's hard teaching about eating his flesh and drinking his blood caused many disciples to desert him and he asked the Twelve if they would also leave, Peter answered, "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life," affirming his belief that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of the living God (John 6:66-69). At the Last Supper, when Jesus began washing the disciples' feet, Peter objected that Jesus should never wash his feet; told that otherwise he would have no part with Jesus, Peter asked to have his hands and head washed too, prompting Jesus to explain that one who is already clean need only have his feet washed (John 13:6-10). When Jesus said he was going where Peter could not yet follow, Peter asked why not, insisting he would lay down his life for him; Jesus replied that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed (John 13:36-38). John's account identifies the servant whose ear Peter cut off at the arrest as Malchus, and notes that Peter's third denial, in the high priest's courtyard, came when a kinsman of Malchus recognized him from the garden (John 18:10, 26). When Mary Magdalene reported the empty tomb, Peter ran there with the disciple Jesus loved, who outran him; Peter went in first and saw the linen cloths lying with the head cloth folded separately (John 20:2-8). After a night of fruitless fishing, Peter and the other disciples obeyed the instruction of a stranger on the shore to cast their net on the right side, catching so many fish that Peter, realizing it was the risen Jesus, girded himself and swam to shore ahead of the boat. After breakfast, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved him, each time charging him to feed his sheep; grieved at being asked a third time, Peter affirmed his love, and Jesus foretold that Peter would die a death that glorified God, then told him simply, "Follow me." When Peter asked about the fate of the disciple Jesus loved, Jesus told him that was not his concern (John 21:1-23). At Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came upon the gathered believers with the sound of wind and tongues of fire, enabling them to speak in other languages, Peter stood up with the Eleven and addressed the bewildered crowd, explaining that this fulfilled Joel's prophecy of the Spirit being poured out on all people. He preached that Jesus of Nazareth, crucified by their hands but raised by God as David had prophesied, was both Lord and Christ; pierced to the heart, the crowd asked what to do, and Peter told them to repent and be baptized, resulting in about three thousand souls added to the believers that day (Acts 2:1-41). Peter, with John, healed a man lame from birth at the temple's Beautiful Gate, saying, "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk"; when the astonished crowd gathered, Peter preached that the man's healing came through faith in Jesus, whom God had raised though the people had denied him, urging them to repent (Acts 3:1-26). Arrested with John and brought before the council, which included Annas, Caiaphas, and other kindred of the high priest, Peter boldly declared that the healed man stood whole by the name of Jesus, "neither is there salvation in any other," leaving the council unable to refute them or punish them for fear of the people, though they ordered the apostles to stop speaking in Jesus's name; Peter and John replied that they could not help speaking what they had seen and heard (Acts 4:1-22). After an angel freed the apostles from prison and they returned to preach in the temple, the high priest's council had them brought before it again and accused them of disobeying the earlier order not to teach in Jesus's name; Peter and the other apostles answered, "We ought to obey God rather than men," and testified that God had exalted the Jesus they had killed as Savior. Enraged, the council was dissuaded from killing them by Gamaliel's counsel, though the apostles were beaten before being released, and left rejoicing to have suffered for Jesus's name (Acts 5:17-42). When the Jerusalem apostles heard Samaria had received the word, they sent Peter and John; Peter rebuked Simon the sorcerer for trying to buy the Holy Spirit's power with money, telling him his heart was not right with God (Acts 8:14-24). Traveling through the region, Peter healed a paralyzed man named Aeneas in Lydda with a word, prompting many there to turn to the Lord. Called to Joppa after the death of a disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas), known for her charity, Peter prayed over her body and raised her back to life, news of which spread and led many in Joppa to believe; he stayed there with a tanner named Simon (Acts 9:32-43). While staying in Joppa, Peter fell into a trance and saw a vision of a sheet lowered from heaven containing all kinds of animals, with a voice telling him to kill and eat; when he protested that he had never eaten anything unclean, the voice told him not to call unclean what God had cleansed, a vision repeated three times. As Peter puzzled over its meaning, messengers arrived from Cornelius, a Roman centurion in Caesarea, whom an angel had instructed to send for Peter; the Spirit told Peter to go with them without hesitation. At Cornelius's house, Peter declared that God had shown him not to call any person unclean, and preached Jesus's life, death, and resurrection to the gathered Gentiles; as he spoke, the Holy Spirit fell on them exactly as it had on the Jewish believers at Pentecost, astonishing Peter's Jewish companions, and Peter had them baptized, recognizing that God accepted people from every nation (Acts 10:1-48). When Jewish believers in Jerusalem criticized Peter for eating with Gentiles at Cornelius's house, he recounted his vision and the Spirit's descent on the Gentiles in detail; hearing this, his critics fell silent and glorified God for granting the Gentiles repentance unto life as well (Acts 11:1-18). After Herod Agrippa I had James executed and imprisoned Peter, intending to bring him to trial, an angel freed Peter from his chains in the night and led him past the guards and through the city gate to freedom. Realizing what had happened, Peter went to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where he surprised the praying believers inside, startling the servant girl Rhoda in the process; he told them to inform James and the brothers, then departed elsewhere. Herod, unable to find him, had the guards executed (Acts 12:1-19).
